# EV Manufacturing and Electric Vehicle Subsidies in India: A Complete Guide to Government Incentives, PLI Schemes, Tax Benefits, and State Policies

### Introduction: India’s EV Policy Now Goes Beyond Just Buying an Electric Vehicle

India’s electric-vehicle story is often reduced to a single question:

“How much subsidy will I get if I buy an EV?”

That question is becoming increasingly outdated.

The more important question today is:

“How much of the EV can India manufacture, how much of the value chain can India localise, and what government support is available at each stage?”

That distinction matters.

An electric vehicle is not merely a vehicle with an electric motor. Behind every EV is an industrial ecosystem involving battery cells, cathode and anode materials, battery management systems, power electronics, motors, controllers, semiconductors, charging equipment, software, testing laboratories, recycling facilities and critical minerals.

India’s EV policy has therefore evolved from consumer-side demand stimulation to a much broader industrial strategy.

The Government of India is now using multiple policy instruments simultaneously:

* Production-linked incentives for automobiles and advanced automotive components
* Production-linked incentives for Advanced Chemistry Cells
* PM E-DRIVE demand incentives
* Incentives for electric buses, trucks and ambulances
* A dedicated manufacturing scheme for electric passenger cars
* Charging-infrastructure support
* Concessional GST
* Customs-duty measures
* State-level capital and fiscal incentives
* Battery-waste and recycling regulations
* Critical-mineral initiatives
* Green-energy and electricity-access measures

The result is a policy framework that resembles a stack rather than a single subsidy.

For an EV manufacturer, the real opportunity may therefore come from combining several layers of support rather than relying on one government scheme.

## 1. The Big Picture: How India Supports the EV Industry

India’s EV incentive ecosystem can broadly be visualised in seven layers:

This is important because different schemes serve different businesses.

A company manufacturing electric scooters is not necessarily eligible for the same incentives as a company manufacturing battery cells.

A global passenger-car manufacturer is also subject to a very different policy architecture from a charging-station operator.

## 2. PM E-DRIVE: India’s Main Demand-Side EV Incentive

The PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM E-DRIVE) scheme is currently one of the most visible components of India’s EV policy.

The scheme was originally notified in September 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,900 crore. Its objective is not restricted to subsidising vehicle purchases; it also covers charging infrastructure, electric buses and development of the EV manufacturing ecosystem.

And there has been an important development in August 2026.

On 10 August 2026, the Ministry of Heavy Industries amended the scheme and increased its total outlay to ₹11,900 crore, while retaining the scheme’s terminal date of 31 March 2028.

That makes PM E-DRIVE particularly relevant for businesses planning their EV strategy today.

### What does PM E-DRIVE support?

The scheme covers multiple categories, including:

* Electric two-wheelers
* Electric three-wheelers
* Electric trucks
* Electric buses
* Electric ambulances
* Public EV charging infrastructure
* Upgradation of EV testing agencies

The original scheme allocated ₹3,679 crore towards demand incentives, ₹4,391 crore towards e-buses, ₹2,000 crore towards EV public charging stations and ₹780 crore towards upgrading testing agencies.

The scheme also uses an Aadhaar-authenticated e-voucher mechanism for eligible vehicle buyers, linking the incentive process to vehicle purchase and OEM claims.

## 3. PM E-DRIVE Is Not One Subsidy - It Is Several Different Programs Under One Umbrella

This is where many articles become misleading.

A manufacturer should not assume that “PM E-DRIVE subsidy” means the same thing for every EV.

The eligibility, vehicle category, manufacturing requirements, price limits, battery requirements and incentive calculations vary by segment.

### Electric Two-Wheelers

The August 2026 amendment provides for support for up to 45,79,120 registered electric two-wheelers under the revised component.

The incentive structure is subject to the notified per-kWh rate and vehicle-level ceiling, with the incentive also subject to the prescribed percentage of ex-factory price. The government has retained the ability to revise the incentive as vehicle costs decline.

The scheme is therefore increasingly moving toward a model where government support reduces as EV economics improve.

That is an important policy signal:

The objective is to use public money to accelerate scale - not permanently subsidise the industry.

## 4. Electric Three-Wheelers

Electric three-wheelers occupy a particularly important position in India’s EV transition because they are used extensively for:

* Last-mile transportation
* Passenger mobility
* Goods delivery
* E-commerce logistics
* Small-business transportation

PM E-DRIVE has supported different categories of electric three-wheelers, including e-rickshaws, e-carts and L5 vehicles.

However, businesses must distinguish between the different sub-categories because eligibility and terminal dates have changed over time.

For example, the L5 three-wheeler segment reached its target and was subsequently closed under the scheme.

This is an important lesson for manufacturers:

Government schemes can close a sub-segment before the headline scheme itself expires.

Therefore, checking only the scheme’s terminal date is not sufficient.

## 5. Electric Trucks: A Newer Opportunity

One of the more strategically important additions to PM E-DRIVE is the electric-truck incentive.

The government allocated ₹500 crore for e-trucks.

But there is a major policy condition.

An eligible e-truck is linked to scrappage of an old vehicle, with a scrapping certificate from a recognised Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facility being required under the scheme framework.

This is more than an EV subsidy.

It combines:

EV adoption + vehicle scrappage + cleaner freight transportation.

That makes the policy especially relevant for:

* Fleet operators
* Logistics companies
* Commercial vehicle manufacturers
* Last-mile delivery businesses
* Freight aggregators
* Vehicle-financing companies

## 6. Electric Ambulances

PM E-DRIVE also created a dedicated ₹500 crore allocation for electric ambulances.

This is a notable expansion of EV policy beyond conventional passenger mobility.

Electric ambulances can potentially reduce operating costs for hospitals and fleet operators while also creating a new specialised EV manufacturing segment.

However, this segment has additional homologation, safety and vehicle-specific requirements.

Therefore, an ambulance manufacturer cannot simply assume that an ordinary electric passenger vehicle automatically qualifies.

## 7. Electric Buses: The Government Is Buying Mobility, Not Just Vehicles

Electric buses represent a fundamentally different EV business model.

Instead of relying entirely on individual consumers, government policy is creating demand through public transport authorities.

PM E-DRIVE provides substantial support for electric buses, while the separate PM e-Bus Sewa-Payment Security Mechanism (PSM) scheme is designed to reduce the payment-default risk faced by OEMs and operators.

The PM e-Bus Sewa-PSM scheme has an outlay of ₹3,435.33 crore and aims to support deployment of more than 38,000 electric buses.

The underlying idea is simple.

For an electric-bus manufacturer, one of the biggest commercial risks is not merely manufacturing the bus.

It is:

“Will the public transport authority actually pay the operator on time?”

The PSM scheme attempts to address precisely that problem by providing payment security mechanisms for eligible public transport arrangements.

This makes the scheme particularly relevant for:

* Bus OEMs
* Fleet operators
* State transport undertakings
* Public transport authorities
* Leasing companies
* EV financiers

## 8. PLI-Auto: The Manufacturing Engine Behind India’s EV Industry

If PM E-DRIVE is primarily associated with demand, PLI-Auto is about building the manufacturing base.

The Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Automobile and Auto Components was approved with a budgetary outlay of approximately ₹25,938 crore.

Its objective is to build manufacturing capabilities for Advanced Automotive Technology products and deepen localisation of the automotive supply chain.

Importantly, the scheme focuses on Zero Emission Vehicles, including:

* Battery Electric Vehicles
* Hydrogen Fuel Cell Vehicles

and advanced automotive technology components.

## 9. What Makes PLI-Auto Different?

PLI-Auto is not simply a capital subsidy.

The government does not generally say:

> “Build a factory and we will reimburse 20% of your factory cost.”

Instead, the PLI framework links incentives to eligible sales and performance.

That changes the business equation.

A manufacturer must think about:

Investment → Production → Sales → Domestic Value Addition → Eligibility → Incentive

rather than simply:

Investment → Subsidy

This is why PLI schemes can be particularly powerful for businesses capable of achieving significant scale.

## 10. PLI-Auto Covers More Than Complete Vehicles

The EV opportunity is not restricted to automobile brands.

PLI-Auto can create opportunities across the advanced automotive component ecosystem.

Potential areas include:

* Battery Management Systems
* Electric drive systems
* Motors
* Power electronics
* Controllers
* Advanced automotive components
* EV-specific assemblies
* Vehicle aggregates
* Advanced drivetrain technologies

The official PLI-Auto framework is designed to support both vehicle manufacturers and advanced automotive component manufacturers.

The latest government data also shows the scale of activity under the scheme: cumulative investment under PLI-Auto had reached ₹44,326 crore by 31 March 2026, with 67,820 jobs reported and ₹2,386.36 crore in incentives disbursed.

That is a useful indicator of where the policy is actually translating into industrial investment.

## 11. PLI-ACC: The Battery Is Where the Real EV Industrial Battle Happens

If India wants to become an EV manufacturing hub, assembling vehicles alone is not enough.

The country also needs to manufacture the battery.

This is why the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage is strategically important.

The government approved the PLI-ACC scheme with an outlay of ₹18,100 crore to establish 50 GWh of domestic Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing capacity.

The scheme aims to reduce India’s dependence on imported battery cells and build domestic manufacturing capability.

## 12. The PLI-ACC Incentive Is Built Around Localisation

The scheme requires beneficiaries to achieve domestic value addition.

The prescribed framework requires domestic value addition to begin at at least 25% and increase to 60% within five years, alongside mandatory investment commitments.

This is critical.

India does not merely want:

“A battery factory located in India.”

It wants:

“A battery value chain located increasingly in India.”

That distinction determines whether the country merely becomes an assembly destination or develops genuine technological and manufacturing depth.

## 13. How Much Battery Capacity Is Actually Being Built?

As of 2026, 40 GWh of the targeted 50 GWh ACC capacity had been awarded to four beneficiary firms.

The beneficiaries include projects associated with:

* ACC Energy Storage
* Ola Cell Technologies
* Reliance New Energy Battery Storage
* Reliance New Energy Battery

The government reported 40 GWh awarded against the 50 GWh target.

But there is an important reality check.

As of July 2026, the government stated that no beneficiary had yet claimed incentive under the PLI-ACC scheme, although the scheme had attracted substantial investment and employment.

This illustrates a crucial point:

An approved incentive is not the same thing as a cash subsidy already received.

For businesses, eligibility, milestones, domestic value addition, production and performance conditions must all be evaluated before treating an incentive as revenue.

## 14. The Battery Opportunity Does Not End With Cells

The development of domestic ACC manufacturing creates opportunities in adjacent industries.

These include:

* Cathode active materials
* Anode active materials
* Electrolytes
* Battery foils
* Separators
* Battery packs
* Battery management systems
* Thermal management
* Battery recycling
* Second-life battery applications

The government has also highlighted the development of supporting battery-material and recycling ecosystems.

For entrepreneurs, this means the EV opportunity may actually be larger in components and infrastructure than in vehicle manufacturing itself.

## 15. SPMEPCI: The Government’s Big Bet on Global Electric-Car Manufacturers

One of the most interesting developments in India’s EV policy is the Scheme to Promote Manufacturing of Electric Passenger Cars in India - SPMEPCI.

The scheme was notified in March 2024 and is designed specifically to attract global electric-passenger-car manufacturers to establish manufacturing operations in India.

This scheme is particularly different from PM E-DRIVE and PLI-Auto.

Its target is not simply:

“Sell more EVs.”

It is:

“Come to India and manufacture them here.”

## 16. SPMEPCI Requires Serious Investment

Approved applicants are required to establish manufacturing facilities in India with a minimum investment of approximately:

### ₹4,150 crore

The facility must be made operational within the prescribed three-year period and achieve:

* Minimum 25% domestic value addition within three years
* Minimum 50% domestic value addition within five years

These requirements make the scheme relevant primarily to serious global or large-scale automotive investors rather than small EV startups.

## 17. The Unusual Incentive Under SPMEPCI

Here is where the scheme becomes particularly interesting.

Approved manufacturers can import eligible electric passenger cars at a 15% customs duty for five years, subject to the scheme’s conditions.

The imported vehicles must have a minimum CIF value of USD 35,000, and the reduced-duty import quantity is capped at 8,000 vehicles per year, with prescribed carry-forward provisions for unused limits.

In other words, the government is effectively saying:

> Establish manufacturing capacity in India, commit to localisation, and in return receive a temporary pathway for limited lower-duty imports.

This is not a traditional subsidy.

It is an investment-for-market-access bargain.

## 18. GST: One of the Simplest EV Incentives

EVs enjoy a major indirect-tax advantage.

Electric vehicles attract 5% GST, significantly below the standard GST treatment applicable to many conventional automobiles.

The GST Council reduced the rate on electric vehicles from 12% to 5%, while chargers and charging stations were also brought down from 18% to 5%.

The benefit is important for both consumers and businesses because the tax advantage affects the overall economics of the EV ecosystem.

It also means that businesses should distinguish between:

* EV itself
* EV charger
* Charging service
* Battery
* EV components
* Manufacturing inputs

because these items do not necessarily all receive identical GST treatment.

## 19. Income-Tax Benefit for EV Buyers: Section 80EEB

There is a commonly repeated EV tax benefit that requires a major qualification.

Section 80EEB of the Income-tax Act provides for a deduction of up to ₹1.50 lakh of interest on a loan taken by an individual for purchasing an electric vehicle.

However, the provision applies to loans sanctioned during the specified period ending 31 March 2023.

Therefore, it should not be marketed in 2026 as a fresh tax deduction available on every new EV loan.

This is a good example of why EV articles copied from older websites can be misleading.

Old EV incentives should not automatically be presented as current incentives.

## 20. Charging Infrastructure: The EV Factory Is Only Half the Story

An EV without charging infrastructure is an industrial product without an ecosystem.

The Ministry of Power issued the Guidelines for Installation and Operation of Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure, 2024.

The guidelines cover charging infrastructure in:

* Private parking
* Offices
* Educational institutions
* Hospitals
* Housing societies
* E-bus depots
* Commercial complexes
* Railway stations
* Airports
* Petrol pumps
* Metro stations
* Municipal parking
* Highways and expressways

This significantly expands the addressable market for charging infrastructure companies.

## 21. Charging-Station Electricity Costs Are Also Being Addressed

The 2024 charging-infrastructure framework provides several measures aimed at making charging stations commercially viable.

These include:

* Specified timelines for electricity connections
* Low-tension connections for eligible loads up to 150 kW
* Access to land through public entities under specified arrangements
* Simplified electricity tariffs
* Single-part tariff framework
* Tariff linked to Average Cost of Supply
* Separate arrangements for residential EV charging

The framework provides for a tariff structure around Average Cost of Supply through 31 March 2028, including lower supply cost during specified solar hours and higher cost during non-solar hours.

This creates an interesting business opportunity:

A charging station is increasingly becoming an energy-management business, not merely a parking-space business.

## 22. PM E-DRIVE Also Supports Public Charging Stations

PM E-DRIVE allocated ₹2,000 crore towards EV public charging infrastructure.

The scheme’s initial framework envisaged support for fast chargers across different vehicle categories, including cars, buses and two-/three-wheelers.

As of July 2026, the government reported approval of ₹689 crore for deployment of 6,562 chargers through three oil marketing companies and nine states.

This creates opportunities for:

* Charging-station developers
* Charger manufacturers
* EPC contractors
* Software companies
* Energy-management platforms
* Battery-swapping businesses
* Fleet-charging operators
* Renewable-energy developers

## 23. The State Government Layer: Where Incentives Can Become Much Larger

This is one of the most overlooked aspects of EV manufacturing.

The Union Government provides national-level schemes.

But a manufacturing project may also qualify for state-level industrial incentives.

These can include:

* Capital subsidy
* SGST reimbursement
* Electricity-duty exemption
* Stamp-duty exemption
* Land concessions
* Employment-linked incentives
* Interest subsidy
* Infrastructure support
* R&D incentives
* Skill-development support
* Registration-fee concessions
* Motor-vehicle-tax concessions
* Charging-infrastructure incentives

The exact benefit depends upon:

State + investment size + district + project category + employment + technology + policy period.

The Ministry of Power has noted that 28 states had notified EV policies providing fiscal and non-fiscal incentives for EV ecosystem development.

Therefore, a manufacturer should never evaluate the economics of an EV factory using only the Central Government schemes.

## 24. Tamil Nadu: A Strong Example of State-Level EV Manufacturing Support

Tamil Nadu’s EV policy provides a good illustration of how state incentives can complement central schemes.

Eligible EV manufacturing projects may choose among specified incentive structures, including:

### SGST reimbursement

Eligible EV OEM projects can receive reimbursement of gross SGST on qualifying EV sales within the state for the prescribed period, subject to investment and employment conditions.

### Turnover-based subsidy

Eligible projects may receive a turnover-linked subsidy subject to prescribed caps.

### Capital subsidy

Eligible EV, EV-component, EVSE and charging-infrastructure projects can receive capital subsidy linked to eligible fixed assets.

### Special ACC capital subsidy

Battery and Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing can receive a separate capital-subsidy framework.

The Tamil Nadu policy provides, for example, a 15% capital subsidy on eligible fixed assets for qualifying EV/EV-component/EVSE/charging projects, while specified ACC projects can access a 20% special capital subsidy, subject to policy conditions.

The important point is not the percentage alone.

It is the ability to combine a national manufacturing strategy with state-level industrial support, subject to the applicable rules.

## 25. Gujarat and Other Manufacturing States

Gujarat’s EV policy also contains separate provisions dealing with:

* EV adoption
* Charging infrastructure
* EV manufacturing
* Component manufacturing

The state has positioned EV manufacturing as part of its broader industrial-investment strategy.

Similarly, states such as:

* Maharashtra
* Karnataka
* Telangana
* Tamil Nadu
* Gujarat
* Andhra Pradesh
* Haryana
* Uttar Pradesh

have developed or operated EV/industrial policies that can be relevant to manufacturing and ecosystem investments.

However, these policies should not be treated as permanent or interchangeable.

The state policy must be checked as of the date of investment approval.

## 26. Why State Selection Can Change the Entire Project Economics

Consider two hypothetical battery manufacturers.

### Company A

Factory in State A:

* Lower land cost
* No capital subsidy
* Higher electricity cost
* Limited infrastructure

### Company B

Factory in State B:

* Industrial land concession
* Capital subsidy
* SGST reimbursement
* Electricity-duty benefit
* Employment incentive
* Faster approvals
* Better logistics

Even if the second location initially appears more expensive, its net project cost and long-term operating economics could be substantially better.

This is why EV manufacturing location strategy should be evaluated using:

Net Capex = Gross Project Cost – Central Incentives – State Incentives – Eligible Tax/Customs Benefits

followed by:

Net Operating Cost = Energy + Labour + Logistics + Tax + Financing + Compliance – Recurring Incentives

That is the real subsidy calculation.

## 27. Battery Waste Management Rules: The Circular-Economy Incentive Layer

EV policy does not end when the vehicle leaves the showroom.

India’s Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 establish an Extended Producer Responsibility framework for batteries.

This has major implications for EV manufacturers and battery companies.

Manufacturers must increasingly think about:

* Collection
* Recycling
* Recovery
* End-of-life batteries
* Traceability
* Producer responsibility
* Recovered materials

The government has specifically identified battery recycling as part of the broader EV ecosystem.

This creates another emerging industry:

EV battery recycling.

A company that can recover lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and other materials from end-of-life batteries may become strategically important to the domestic EV ecosystem.

## 28. National Critical Mineral Mission: The Incentive Behind the Incentive

There is another layer that is easy to miss.

EV batteries require critical minerals.

India therefore cannot build a resilient EV industry merely by manufacturing battery packs.

It needs access to:

* Lithium
* Cobalt
* Nickel
* Graphite
* Rare earth elements
* Other critical minerals

The Government’s National Critical Mineral Mission, approved in January 2025, is designed to strengthen the critical-mineral value chain, covering areas from exploration and mining to processing and recovery from end-of-life products.

This is strategically important because battery manufacturing economics are ultimately linked to raw-material security.

## 29. Customs Policy: The Less Visible EV Incentive

Customs policy can be just as important as a headline subsidy.

The government has used tariff policy to influence:

* Battery manufacturing
* Critical minerals
* EV components
* Manufacturing equipment
* Electric passenger vehicles

The SPMEPCI is the clearest example, where reduced customs duty on eligible imported electric passenger cars is linked to investment and domestic manufacturing commitments.

For manufacturers, therefore, the right question is not simply:

“Is there a subsidy?”

It should also be:

“What is the effective landed cost of my imported inputs after applicable customs and GST treatment?”

## 30. Testing and Homologation Infrastructure

EVs introduce technologies that traditional automotive testing infrastructure was not originally designed around.

PM E-DRIVE therefore allocated ₹780 crore for upgrading testing agencies.

The ecosystem includes major testing institutions such as:

* ARAI
* ICAT
* NATRAX
* GARC

The objective is to strengthen testing capabilities for emerging vehicle technologies.

This is important for startups because certification and homologation can otherwise become a significant time and cost barrier.

## 31. 100% FDI: An Additional Advantage for Global EV Investors

India permits 100% FDI under the automatic route in the automobile sector, subject to the applicable foreign-investment framework.

This becomes particularly relevant when combined with:

* PLI-Auto
* SPMEPCI
* State industrial incentives
* Domestic manufacturing requirements
* India’s growing EV market

Investors therefore have a relatively broad pathway for establishing Indian EV manufacturing operations.

## 32. The Government Is Moving From “Subsidise the Vehicle” to “Build the Ecosystem”

This is perhaps the most important conclusion from India’s EV incentive architecture.

The first generation of EV policy focused heavily on:

“Make the EV cheaper.”

The current policy is increasingly focused on:

“Make the EV ecosystem Indian.”

That means:

### Cells

Manufacture batteries domestically.

### Components

Develop motors, controllers, BMS and advanced automotive systems.

### Vehicles

Build complete EVs in India.

### Charging

Build charging infrastructure.

### Public transport

Deploy electric buses.

### Freight

Electrify trucks.

### Recycling

Recover materials from old batteries.

### Minerals

Secure critical raw materials.

### Technology

Develop domestic testing and R&D capability.

This is an industrial-policy transformation rather than merely an environmental subsidy programme.

## 33. What Incentives Are Available to Different EV Businesses?

A practical way to understand the ecosystem is to look at the business model.

The word “where eligible” is critical.

A scheme being relevant to an industry does not automatically make every company in that industry eligible.

## 34. FAME-II: Important, But No Longer the Current Demand Scheme

A large number of articles still present FAME-II as if it is India’s current EV subsidy programme.

It is not.

FAME-II operated from 1 April 2019 to 31 March 2024, with an outlay of ₹11,500 crore.

It was followed by the Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme and then PM E-DRIVE.

This distinction is important for businesses preparing:

* Investor decks
* Project reports
* Bank proposals
* Subsidy applications
* Government representations
* Website content
* Tax opinions

Historical subsidy figures should not be presented as current entitlements.

## 35. EMPS 2024: The Short Bridge Between FAME-II and PM E-DRIVE

The Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme 2024 was introduced as an interim measure before PM E-DRIVE.

It had a much smaller outlay and limited duration.

It was subsequently subsumed into PM E-DRIVE.

Therefore, it is mainly relevant for understanding the policy transition rather than as a current standalone incentive.

## 36. What an EV Manufacturer Should Actually Do Before Setting Up a Factory

The biggest mistake would be to begin with:

“Which subsidy can I get?”

The better approach is:

### Step 1 - Identify the product

Is it:

* EV
* Battery
* Cell
* Motor
* Controller
* Charger
* BMS
* Component
* Charging station
* Recycling facility?

### Step 2 - Identify the manufacturing category

Determine whether the product falls within the eligible categories of:

* PLI-Auto
* PLI-ACC
* SPMEPCI
* State EV policy
* State industrial policy

### Step 3 - Calculate Domestic Value Addition

This is increasingly important.

Government support is becoming closely linked to localisation.

### Step 4 - Build a scheme-compliant investment plan

Do not build the project first and ask about eligibility later.

### Step 5 - Compare states

Evaluate:

* Land
* Power
* SGST
* Capital subsidy
* Stamp duty
* Electricity duty
* Employment benefits
* Infrastructure
* Logistics
* Water
* Ports
* Supplier ecosystem

### Step 6 - Model the incentive cash flow

An approved subsidy may not be immediately received.

Therefore, the financial model should distinguish:

Capex incurred → Eligibility achieved → Claim filed → Incentive approved → Incentive received

### Step 7 - Track compliance

PLI schemes are performance-linked.

Missing:

* investment milestones,
* domestic value addition,
* production requirements,
* sales criteria,
* testing requirements,
* documentation,

can materially affect incentive eligibility.

## 37. The Most Important Financial Question: “Subsidy” or “Deferred Economics”?

An incentive should never automatically be treated as free money.

Suppose an EV manufacturer invests ₹1,000 crore.

If it receives a ₹100 crore eligible incentive, the project does not necessarily mean:

₹1,000 crore investment – ₹100 crore = ₹900 crore immediately.

The company may have to:

* Meet investment thresholds
* Achieve production
* Sell eligible products
* Maintain domestic value addition
* Meet localisation requirements
* File claims
* Obtain certification
* Wait for disbursement

Therefore, the incentive should be modelled as a conditional future cash flow.

That is particularly important for project finance.

## 38. A Better Way to Think About EV Subsidies

India’s EV incentives can be divided into three economic categories.

### Category A - Demand Incentives

These make EVs cheaper for the buyer.

Example:

PM E-DRIVE

### Category B - Production Incentives

These reward companies for building and selling eligible products in India.

Examples:

PLI-Auto

PLI-ACC

### Category C - Investment Incentives

These make it more attractive to establish a manufacturing operation in a particular location or under a particular policy.

Examples:

SPMEPCI

State EV policies

State industrial incentives

This three-part classification makes India’s EV policy much easier to understand.

## 39. What About EV Startups?

EV startups should not assume that the largest schemes are automatically designed for them.

A startup manufacturing:

* Battery-swapping equipment
* Fleet software
* BMS
* Charging software
* EV components
* Small commercial EVs
* Battery recycling technology

may benefit more from state-level incentives, MSME schemes, R&D support, manufacturing incentives or component-level policies than from large vehicle-specific PLI schemes.

The startup should therefore begin with its technology and product classification, not with the subsidy list.

## 40. The Opportunity Is Bigger Than EV Manufacturing

The EV sector is creating several parallel industries.

### EV manufacturing

Cars, buses, trucks, 2W and 3W.

### Battery manufacturing

Cells, modules and packs.

### Charging

AC chargers, DC fast chargers and charging networks.

### Software

Fleet management, charging management, energy optimisation and diagnostics.

### Components

Motors, inverters, controllers, BMS and thermal-management systems.

### Recycling

Battery collection and material recovery.

### Finance

EV leasing, fleet financing and battery financing.

### Energy

Renewable-energy-powered charging.

### After-sales

Battery diagnostics, repair and refurbishment.

This means an entrepreneur does not necessarily need to build an EV to participate in India’s EV economy.

## 41. The EV Policy Opportunity in One Diagram

A useful way to understand the ecosystem is:

Critical Minerals

↓

Battery Materials

↓

ACC Cells

↓

Battery Packs + BMS

↓

Motors + Power Electronics + Components

↓

EV Manufacturing

↓

Charging Infrastructure

↓

Consumers + Fleets + Public Transport

↓

Battery Collection

↓

Recycling

↓

Recovered Critical Materials

↓

Back Into Manufacturing

This is the circular industrial ecosystem India is gradually trying to create.

## 43. What Businesses Should Not Assume

There are several myths around EV subsidies.

### Myth 1: Every EV receives a government subsidy.

Incorrect.

Eligibility depends on the applicable scheme, vehicle category, date, certification, manufacturing conditions and available funds.

### Myth 2: FAME-II is still India’s main EV subsidy.

Incorrect.

FAME-II ended in March 2024.

### Myth 3: PLI means the government pays for the factory.

Incorrect.

PLI is performance-linked and involves specific eligibility and production/sales conditions.

### Myth 4: Every EV component gets the same tax treatment as an EV.

Incorrect.

GST and customs treatment must be evaluated product-by-product.

### Myth 5: Central incentives are enough to decide factory location.

Incorrect.

State incentives can materially change project economics.

### Myth 6: An approved incentive equals immediate cash.

Incorrect.

Disbursement normally depends upon meeting applicable milestones and claim requirements.

## 44. The Strategic Direction for 2026–2030

India’s EV policy appears to be entering its next phase.

The earlier policy question was:

How do we create demand?

The emerging question is:

How do we create industrial depth?

The next phase is likely to be shaped by:

* Battery-cell localisation
* Critical-mineral security
* Domestic components
* EV exports
* Electric commercial vehicles
* Charging infrastructure
* Battery recycling
* Public transport electrification
* Advanced automotive electronics
* Energy-storage integration

The August 2026 PM E-DRIVE amendment, which raises the scheme outlay to ₹11,900 crore while continuing support through March 2028, reinforces the government’s continuing emphasis on electric mobility.

## 45. Conclusion

India’s EV incentive framework should not be viewed as a single subsidy.

It is a multi-layered industrial strategy.

At one end, PM E-DRIVE attempts to stimulate vehicle adoption.

At the manufacturing level, PLI-Auto encourages advanced automotive production.

Behind the vehicle, PLI-ACC attempts to create domestic battery-cell capacity.

For global car manufacturers, SPMEPCI creates a framework linking market access with manufacturing investment and localisation.

For public transport, PM e-Bus Sewa-PSM attempts to make electric-bus deployment more financially bankable.

For charging companies, the Ministry of Power’s charging-infrastructure framework attempts to make electricity access, tariffs and land arrangements more predictable.

At the state level, additional incentives can materially influence where factories are established.

And beyond the vehicle itself, the government is gradually building policy support around critical minerals, battery recycling, charging infrastructure and the wider clean-mobility ecosystem.

The real EV opportunity in India, therefore, is not simply:

“Manufacture an electric vehicle and claim a subsidy.”

It is:

“Build a business that sits inside India’s localisation, electrification and clean-mobility value chain.”

For manufacturers, investors and entrepreneurs, the strongest strategy is to map the entire project against Central Government incentives + State incentives + tax treatment + customs structure + localisation requirements + financing + compliance obligations before committing capital.

That is where the difference between an ordinary EV project and a truly incentive-efficient EV project is created.

### TwoTax Perspective

The EV sector is moving rapidly from a subsidy-led market to a manufacturing-led ecosystem.

For businesses entering this sector, incentive planning should therefore happen before the investment decision rather than after the factory is established.

A proper EV project assessment should cover:

* Central Government scheme eligibility
* PLI applicability
* Domestic Value Addition requirements
* State-specific incentives
* GST and customs implications
* Land and infrastructure benefits
* Battery and EPR compliance
* Charging-infrastructure regulations
* Capital expenditure planning
* Incentive-disbursement timelines
* Financial modelling of conditional incentives
* Ongoing regulatory and documentation compliance

The biggest EV incentive is not necessarily the largest subsidy. It is the policy combination that produces the strongest project economics.

results.page_content:
### **Policy Update Shivani Chauhan**

### **Background:**

India’s electric vehicle (EV) market needed a safety net. In September 2024, two government programmes that had been subsidising EV purchases naming FAME-I and FAME-II, came to an end. Without a replacement, the fear was that EV sales would slow down and the push towards cleaner transport would lose steam.

To prevent that, the Union Cabinet approved the PM E-DRIVE scheme (Prime Minister Electric-Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement) with a budget of ₹10,900 crore. It was officially launched on 1 October 2024. The scheme has three straightforward goals: get more people buying electric vehicles, reduce India’s dependence on imported oil, and cut down air pollution in cities.

Originally planned to run for two years, the scheme has since been extended to four years, now ending on 31 March 2028, with no extra money added to the budget. Subsidies for electric two-wheelers run until July 2026, and support for electric three-wheelers (e-rickshaws and e-carts) continues until March 2028

### **Functioning:**

PM E-DRIVE is not just about giving discounts on EVs. It also funds charging stations and upgrades the labs that test and certify electric vehicles. Here is how the main parts work.

*The Subsidy: How Buyers Actually Benefit*

When you buy an eligible EV, you do not apply for a subsidy separately and wait for a cheque. The discount is applied at the time of purchase. Here is the process:

1. You visit a registered dealer and choose your EV.
2. You complete a quick Aadhaar face verification on the PM E-DRIVE portal at the dealership.
3. The dealer generates a digital voucher (e-voucher), which both you and the dealer sign.
4. The dealer uploads this voucher. The manufacturer then claims the subsidy amount back from the government through the portal.

In short: you pay less upfront, and the government settles the difference with the manufacturer later. For companies or fleet operators buying multiple vehicles, the process is the same, the portal generates the voucher directly for them.

*How Much Subsidy Do You Get?*

The incentive is either up to 15 per cent of the vehicle’s factory price, or a fixed per-vehicle cap whichever is lower. This means the absolute benefit is higher on more expensive vehicles, but the government caps how much any single vehicle can receive.

*Charging Stations*

One of the biggest reasons people hesitate to buy EVs is ‘range anxiety’, the worry that they will run out of charge with nowhere to recharge. PM E-DRIVE tackles this directly by offering a one-time payment to businesses and operators who install approved public charging stations. The focus is on highways, bus depots, government buildings, and busy urban areas. The idea is to use government money to encourage private investment in charging infrastructure.  
The scheme targets around 72,300 EV charging stations and battery-swapping facilities across the country, backed by a ₹2,000 crore allocation.

*Manufacturing and Testing*

To prevent the subsidy from benefiting imported components, the scheme is linked to a Phased Manufacturing Programme (PMP). Manufacturers must source a set percentage of vehicle parts locally including from small businesses (MSMEs) to remain eligible. An additional ₹780 crore has been set aside to upgrade the labs that test and certify EVs and batteries, so India can do this work domestically rather than relying on overseas testing.

### **Performance:**

The numbers so far are encouraging and in some ways, better than expected.

*Sales*

A study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) found that in its first year, PM E-DRIVE supported the sale of around 11.3 lakh EVs annually, about 3.4 times the yearly sales seen under FAME-II. What makes this more impressive is that the per-unit subsidy under PM E-DRIVE (₹5,000 per kWh) is roughly half of what FAME-II offered (₹10,000 per kWh). More buyers, less money per buyer, that is a sign the market is growing on its own.

By early 2026, the scheme had supported 22.12 lakh vehicle sales: 19.19 lakh electric two-wheelers and 2.93 lakh electric three-wheelers.

*Government Spending*

Of the total ₹10,900 crore budget, approximately ₹1,703 crore had been reimbursed to manufacturers by end-December 2025, only for two- and three-wheelers so far. The bulk of the budget remains to be deployed, particularly for e-buses and charging infrastructure.

*Electric Buses*

₹4,391 crore has been set aside to bring 14,028 electric buses to seven cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Pune, and Surat. Tenders for over 10,900 buses have already been finalised (Phase I), and tenders for the remaining ~2,900 buses (Phase II) were floated in early 2026. This is the part of the scheme with the most direct impact on public transport and urban air quality.

The scheme has supported over 28 lakh EVs in total, according to government figures. The real test, however, is not just how many vehicles are sold but whether the charging network keeps pace, and whether the gains are spread evenly across cities and income groups*.*



Source: PM E-DRIVE Portal, Ministry of Heavy Industries, Government of India

### **Impact:**

*For Buyers*

The most visible impact is in the two and three-wheeler market. For auto-rickshaw drivers, delivery workers, and daily commuters, an e-rickshaw or electric scooter is often a livelihood vehicle, not a lifestyle choice. Lower purchase costs through the subsidy, combined with lower fuel costs (electricity vs petrol), make a tangible difference to household budgets. The scheme’s design with the discount applied at the point of sale also means buyers do not need to navigate a complex reimbursement process.

*For Cities*

The e-bus programme is where the public-good impact is most direct. Electric buses in major cities mean quieter, cleaner roads and lower emissions from public transport, a sector that has historically been difficult to decarbonise. The OPEX model used (where the government pays for operations rather than requiring state transport bodies to buy buses upfront) removes a major financial barrier for cash-strapped state transport corporations.

*For Industry*

By tying subsidies to domestic manufacturing requirements, the scheme creates incentives for Indian EV makers and component suppliers to grow. The testing-lab upgrades also mean manufacturers no longer need to send vehicles abroad for certification, which saves time and money and builds long-term technical capacity in India.

*Where the Gaps are?*

The gains so far are concentrated in cheaper vehicle categories, two and three-wheelers, where the subsidy is easy to apply and consumer demand already exists. Electric buses and trucks, which have the potential for the deepest long-term impact, are moving more slowly because they involve complex procurement, state capacity, and infrastructure readiness.

High sales numbers also do not automatically mean high quality of impact. If charging infrastructure does not keep up with vehicle sales, new EV owners will face the very range anxiety the scheme is trying to solve. And if the grid is not clean, electric vehicles are only as green as the electricity that powers them.

### **Way Forward:**

To consolidate and build upon PM E-DRIVE’s early achievements, the next phase of the scheme should pursue several interconnected priorities.

*Make Subsidies Smarter*

Rather than a flat subsidy for all buyers, the next phase should direct more support to lower-income buyers, rural users, and segments where EVs are not yet commercially viable without help. A delivery worker buying an e-rickshaw needs more support than a middle-class urban buyer replacing a petrol scooter.

*Prioritise Charging Infrastructure Quality*

The target of 72,300 charging stations is ambitious. But the number of chargers matters less than whether they work reliably. Investment in maintenance, grid connectivity, and uptime monitoring should accompany the rollout, not follow it years later.

*Strengthen the Manufacturing Link*

The domestic component requirements are a step in the right direction, but more can be done to ensure that smaller suppliers and MSMEs actually benefit, rather than just large OEMs satisfying the letter of the requirement through subsidiary sourcing.

*Track What Actually Matters*

The government currently measures success mainly through vehicle sales figures. A more complete picture would track actual vehicle usage, emissions reductions, charging-station uptime, and battery recycling, outcomes that reveal whether the transition to electric mobility is real, or just a shift in what vehicles are sold on paper.

PM E-DRIVE has made a strong start. The real challenge now is ensuring that the infrastructure, the supply chain, and the policy commitment keep pace with the sales numbers, so that the early momentum translates into a lasting shift, and not just a subsidy-driven spike.
